turns.prompt_text: I have a whole ton of beehive frame foundation with wax on it We couldn't use it because the wax was too dark or it had drone brood sized cells So now we have many tubs of them I would like to reuse them by melting the wax off or just removing the wax somehow. I'm just not sure how I have some in a Crock-Pot but the Crock-Pot isn't big enough and I had to cut each frame in half just to get them in It is, however, effective at melting the wax Once it is done, the the black residue still remains and I scrape it off with a hive tool but I'm unsure if any wax is contained within it I'm just looking for the best way to extract the wax Preferably keeping the frames as well I think the best solution would be a dedicated enclosure
turns.response_html:
That black residue left behind is called slumgum—a mix of old pupal cocoons, propolis, pollen, and bee debris. Old brood comb is like a sponge; slumgum can trap up to 20–30% of the total wax unless heat and drainage work together.

For processing full frames in bulk without cutting or destroying them, a dedicated steam wax melter or a solar wax melter is the standard approach.

Method 1: DIY Steam Box (Fastest Bulk Method)

Steam melts the wax rapidly at ~100°C (212°F), safely below the scorch point of beeswax, while sanitizing the frames.

  • The Enclosure: Stack one or two standard hive bodies over a collection funnel/tray, or use an insulated wooden box sized to hang 8–10 full frames.
  • The Heat Source: An inexpensive commercial wallpaper steamer (Wagner or similar) piped via a brass fitting into the side or top of the box.
  • Drainage & Catch: Place a metal mesh screen beneath the frames to catch the bulk slumgum. The melted wax and condensed water drain out a bottom spout into a collection bucket.
  • Separation: Because wax floats on water, it solidifies into a clean cake on top of the condensed water as it cools.

Method 2: Solar Wax Melter (Zero Energy, Hands-Off)

Best for steady processing during sunny months.

  • The Setup: An insulated, black-lined box with a double-pane glass or polycarbonate lid angled toward the sun.
  • Operation: Frames sit on a tilted metal drip tray lined with paper towels or mesh. The wax melts, filters through the mesh, and collects in a bread pan at the bottom.
  • Pros & Cons: Produces beautifully bleached, light wax naturally, but processes only 2–4 frames at a time.

Frame & Foundation Handling

  • Plastic Foundation: If you have one-piece plastic frames or plastic foundation sheets (e.g., Rite-Cell/Acorn), steam will strip the wax cleanly without melting the underlying plastic (high-density polypropylene withstands ~120°C). Once steamed, let them cool, scrape any residual slumgum with a hive tool, and recoat with melted wax using a foam roller.
  • Wood Frames with Wax Foundation: The wax runs off completely. You can scrape the remaining wire/groove and pop in new foundation sheets.

turns.prompt_text: So I already have this deep Hive box which I spray painted black and I have a few layers of mesh beneath it and then I have a large tray pan which is metal at the bottom On top I have another lid made out of wood bars which hold some glass from fish tanks. I imagine I could use this Right now it is set up as a solar heater but I wonder if we could apply steam as well somehow We also have a corded heat gun. Maybe we could get it kick-started somehow
turns.response_html:
You already have about 80% of a functional rig built. Adding steam to that existing deep box is straightforward, but skip the heat gun.

A heat gun blows dry, focused air between 300°C and 600°C (570°F–1100°F). Beeswax has a flash point around 204°C (400°F) and discolors/scorches above 85°C (185°F). A heat gun will warp plastic foundation, scorch the wax, create toxic vapor, and pose a severe fire hazard.

Adapting Your Box for Steam

To convert your solar box into a high-throughput steam melter, you only need to swap the top and inject steam:

  • Swap the Glass for Wood/Insulation: Do not use the fish tank glass lid with steam. Non-tempered aquarium glass can shatter from thermal shock, and glass loses heat too quickly for steam to remain efficient. Top the box with a solid wooden outer cover or a piece of plywood with rigid foam board underneath.
  • Add a Steam Port: Drill a 1/2-inch to 3/4-inch hole in the upper side of the deep box (near the top frame rest). Screw in a threaded brass barb or compression fitting connected to a standard wallpaper steamer hose.
  • Drainage & Catch: Keep your mesh screen in place beneath the frames to catch the slumgum. Elevate the box slightly on blocks so the melted wax and condensed hot water drain freely from your bottom metal pan into an external bucket.
  • Run Time: A batch of 8–10 deep frames typically melts completely clean within 30 to 45 minutes of active steaming.

Operating as a Hybrid System

  • Sunny Days (Solar Mode): Keep the glass lid on, angle the box toward the sun at roughly 30–45 degrees, and let it run passively. It’s slow, but it acts as a zero-cost solar bleaching setup.
  • Bulk/Cloudy Days (Steam Mode): Pop on the insulated solid lid, plug in the steam boiler, and strip a full box of frames every hour.

turns.prompt_text: So we are essentially building a sauna here If we put essentially a plank of wood on top of it to cover it, I also ratchet strap. It closed the entire thing so that it's very well sealed And if we have a hole somewhere in the deep towards the top where we can let hot steam in from boiling water Then we just need some kind of thermometer check to make sure it's getting hot enough I really don't believe it will have the potential to become overly hot, but we could check for that too
turns.response_html:
Yes, "sauna" is the exact right mental model.

A few critical adjustments to your plan:

1. Do Not Make It Airtight (Crucial for Safety)

Ratchet-strapping the box closed is great to keep the pieces physically aligned, but do not seal it so tightly that steam cannot escape.

  • The Physics: Steam expands dramatically. If you inject pressurized steam into a sealed box with no exhaust, pressure builds up until the box blows a seam or pops the steam hose off violently.
  • The Fix: Let the steam vent naturally. The drainage spout/pan at the bottom should remain wide open so condensed water and liquid wax drain immediately, which also doubles as an exhaust vent. If steam is rolling out of the bottom drain alongside hot wax, your internal temperature is right where it needs to be.

2. Overheating & Temperature Monitoring

You are correct—it physically cannot overheat.

  • In an unpressurized vessel, wet steam caps the internal ambient temperature at 100°C (212°F).
  • Beeswax melts between 62°C and 65°C (144°F–149°F) and doesn't scorch until well above 120°C (250°F).
  • Standard plastic foundation (polypropylene) withstands continuous heat up to 120°C–130°C before softening.

A standard dial meat thermometer poked through a small pilot hole near the bottom/middle will let you verify that the internal chamber reaches at least 70°C–80°C (160°F–175°F), which is plenty hot to get a rapid, clean melt without running the boiler dry.

Practical Operating Tips

  • Add Water to the Catch Bucket: Put 2–3 inches of warm water in your collection bucket beneath the drain pan before starting. The melted wax will drop in, float on the water surface, and cool into a smooth, easily removable cake without sticking to the plastic bucket.
  • Insulate the Exterior: Standard 3/4" pine loses heat rapidly through the sides. Wrapping the outside of your deep box in a layer of foil-faced bubble wrap or foam board will cut your steam cycle time in half.

turns.prompt_text: So where am I going to find a water boil steamer system to create the steam?
turns.response_html:
The gold standard tool that beekeepers use for this is a standard electric wallpaper steamer.

You don't need dedicated beekeeping equipment—wallpaper steamers are built specifically to boil water continuously and pump low-pressure, high-volume steam through a flexible hose for 60 to 90 minutes on a single fill.

Where to Get One

  • Big-Box Hardware Stores: Home Depot, Lowe's, Menards, or Ace Hardware carry the Wagner 725 (or Wagner 715/915) wallpaper steamer for around $50–$75 in the paint/wallpaper aisle.
  • Online (Amazon / eBay): Search for "wallpaper steamer" or "electric steam generator." (The basic Wagner models or unbranded versions are widely available).
  • Equipment Rental Stores: Sunbelt Rentals, United Rentals, or local tool rental counters usually rent them for ~$15–$20/day if you just want to do one massive weekend batch.
  • Secondary Market: Check Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, or local estate sales. People buy them for one home renovation project and sell them for $15–$30.

How to Hook It Up to Your Box

  1. Remove the Steam Plate: The steamer comes with a flat plastic plate used for pressing against drywall. Unscrew or unclip the plate from the end of the flexible hose.
  2. Plumbing to the Deep:
    • The hose end usually has a threaded fitting (often 1/4-inch or 3/8-inch standard pipe/compression thread).
    • Drill a matching hole into the upper side of your wooden deep box.
    • Thread in a cheap brass hose barb or pipe nipple from the plumbing aisle, and attach the steam hose directly to it.
  3. Run Cycle: Fill the steamer reservoir with tap or distilled water, plug it into a standard 120V outlet (ideally on a 15A or 20A circuit, as they draw ~1500W), and it will start pumping rolling steam into your deep box in about 10–15 minutes.
